primary_coaching_focus.topic: Re-routing qualification when the answering party discloses they aren't the right contact
primary_coaching_focus.quote: I have memory problems, so I don't pay a lot of bills.
primary_coaching_focus.why: Doug signals from 00:37 onward that his wife handles the bills, and explicitly discloses memory problems at 01:45, yet the rep keeps running qualifiers on Doug for another two-plus minutes before finally agreeing to call the wife directly at 04:47. Earlier recognition would have saved call time and produced cleaner data.

key_moments.quote: I'm 74. I'm retired, and I'm on a limited income.
key_moments.stewart_read: Retired with both spouses now home full-time and running a 1,500 sq ft shop/garage in addition to the house is a strong usage-increase signal — exactly the kind of anchor the interest_question section is designed to surface.

key_moments.quote: Probably she pays all the bills. I have memory problems, so I don't pay a lot of bills.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is a trust-gift disclosure per the schema's vulnerability framing — Doug is telling the rep, unprompted, that he is not a reliable respondent. The rep's reply ('You're good. Yeah. No worries.') is a generic reassurance, not an acknowledgment-plus-bridge.

key_moments.quote: I guess one of the main requirements for getting solar is having a credit score above 650.
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep states a core qualifying threshold with 'I guess,' undercutting the requirement's authority, and asks a memory-impaired, non-bill-paying customer to self-report a number he plainly cannot know. The schema's own spencer_operator_note raises the open policy question of whether setters should be DQing on stated credit at all — this call is a clean example of why that policy matters, since Doug's answer ('Probably she pays all the bills... I don't pay a lot of bills') is not a usable data point for a DQ decision either way.
